ARCHITECTURE CONTEXT (decided — do not modify this block):
  ARCHITECTURE DECISION RECORD (ADR)
  Project: Jhaz-imprints E-Commerce Platform
  Date: 2026-04-25
  Status: DECIDED
  
  --- PRE-SCORING REASONING ---
  
  Five forces shaped the evaluation before any option was written:
  
    Force 1 — Team size and familiarity. A small JS team means operational
    overhead is expensive. Every additional service to deploy, monitor, and
    debug is a multiplier on cognitive load. Simplicity has disproportionate
    value here.
  
    Force 2 — The automated order pipeline is the core feature. It touches
    transactional data (orders, payments — relational, strict integrity) AND
    flexible catalog data (fabric/style attributes that vary per garment
    category). This dual-data-nature is real and shapes the database choice.
  
    Force 3 — SEO is a growth lever, not a nice-to-have. Jhaz-imprints
    competes against large marketplaces in search. If product pages are not
    server-rendered, Google cannot index them and organic traffic — the
    cheapest marketing channel — is lost. This makes the frontend choice
    load-bearing.
  
    Force 4 — Near-zero infra budget. Eliminates Kubernetes, self-hosted
    brokers, and dedicated VMs. Must fit on free-tier or pay-per-request
    services: Neon, Railway hobby tier, Atlas M0, Upstash Redis, Vercel.
  
    Force 5 — No microservices experience on the team. Distributed tracing,
    service discovery, inter-service auth are out of scope. Any option
    requiring true microservices will produce a poor result regardless of
    theoretical merit.
  
  --- OPTION A: Integrated Monolith ---
  
  Description: One Node.js/Express application handles all routes — auth,
  catalog, orders, payments, notifications, admin. Connects to both PostgreSQL
  (Prisma) and MongoDB (Mongoose) from a single process. Frontend is a Vite
  React SPA served from CDN. No separate packages — flat folder structure
  (src/routes, src/services, src/models). Fastest path to a running app but
  the SPA is client-rendered, meaning poor SEO unless SSR is retrofitted later.
  
  Scores:
    (a) Time-to-ship:          9/10 — least setup, no tooling overhead
    (b) Scalability:           4/10 — single process; must duplicate whole
                                      server to scale any one concern
    (c) Operational simplicity: 9/10 — one deployment, one log stream
    (d) SEO/marketing:         3/10 — Vite SPA serves empty shell to crawlers
  
  Total: 25/40
  
  Top 2 risks:
    - SEO is broken by default. Retrofitting SSR onto a mature SPA is a
      painful, expensive refactor that delays marketing impact indefinitely.
    - Without package boundaries, order pipeline, notification, and product
      logic bleed together. By sprint 4 the codebase resists change.
  
  --- OPTION B: Modular Monorepo (Next.js storefront + Express API) ---
  
  Description: A pnpm workspace monorepo with clear package boundaries:
  apps/web (Next.js 14 App Router — SSR storefront), apps/admin (Vite React —
  internal tool, SEO irrelevant), packages/api (Express.js — all business
  logic), packages/db (Prisma + PostgreSQL), packages/catalog-db (Mongoose +
  MongoDB), packages/shared (Zod schemas, TypeScript types). API is a single
  Express process. Notifications run on BullMQ backed by Upstash Redis.
  Storefront is fully server-rendered so every product page is indexable.
  Admin stays as a lightweight Vite SPA. Two deployments, not ten.
  
  Scores:
    (a) Time-to-ship:          7/10 — monorepo tooling adds ~1–2 days setup;
                                      pays back within sprint 2
    (b) Scalability:           8/10 — API and storefront scale independently;
                                      BullMQ decouples notifications from HTTP
    (c) Operational simplicity: 7/10 — two deployments (Vercel + Railway);
                                      shared types eliminate layer drift
    (d) SEO/marketing:         9/10 — Next.js App Router gives SSR + static
                                      generation, metadata API, sitemap built in
  
  Total: 31/40
  
  Top 2 risks:
    - Monorepo tooling learning curve. Engineers unfamiliar with pnpm
      workspaces and Turborepo caching may lose time configuring the build
      pipeline. Mitigate by providing a starter template.
    - Two databases increase cognitive surface area. A clear rule must be
      documented and enforced: transactional data → Postgres, flexible catalog
      → Mongo. Enforce in code review.
  
  --- OPTION C: Light Service Split (separate Order Processing Service) ---
  
  Description: Next.js storefront (SSR, same as Option B), a primary Express
  API for auth, catalog, and user management, and a SECOND Express service
  dedicated to the order pipeline — order creation, payment webhook handling,
  BullMQ jobs, notifications. Two services share the same PostgreSQL and
  MongoDB instances. Deployed as separate Railway services. Appears to offer
  cleaner separation of concerns but introduces distributed systems problems
  (service-to-service auth, inter-service timeouts, cross-service log
  debugging) with no benefit relevant at this stage of product.
  
  Scores:
    (a) Time-to-ship:          4/10 — inter-service communication, service
                                      discovery, shared type contracts add weeks
    (b) Scalability:           9/10 — order service scales independently;
                                      correct shape at higher scale
    (c) Operational simplicity: 3/10 — two API services to deploy, monitor,
                                      debug; no distributed tracing in scope
    (d) SEO/marketing:         9/10 — identical Next.js storefront to Option B
  
  Total: 25/40
  
  Top 2 risks:
    - Premature distribution. At Jhaz-imprints' launch volume the separate
      order service adds complexity not justified until 12–18 months of strong
      growth.
    - Debugging across service boundaries without distributed tracing will
      consume disproportionate time in a small team.
  
  --- COMPARATIVE SUMMARY ---
  
    Option A: Integrated Monolith    — 25/40
    Option B: Modular Monorepo       — 31/40  ← HIGHEST
    Option C: Light Service Split    — 25/40
  
  --- SELECTION RATIONALE ---
  
  Option B scores highest at 31/40 and is the correct choice for this context.
  The two-point penalty on time-to-ship versus Option A is recovered within
  sprint 1 once the monorepo scaffold is in place — Turborepo caching reduces
  redundant builds, and shared Zod schemas between API and storefront eliminate
  a whole class of type-drift bugs across every subsequent sprint.
  
  The critical differentiator is SEO. Option A's 3/10 on SEO is a structural
  disqualifier for a business whose primary growth channel is organic search
  for terms like "Nigerian wedding aso-oke tailor" or "African traditional
  dress online." Option C achieves the same SEO score as Option B but costs
  4 points on time-to-ship and 4 points on operational simplicity with no
  benefit relevant at this stage.
  
  The two-database approach is a deliberate, justified trade-off. Transactional
  integrity of orders and payments cannot be compromised. Schema flexibility
  for garment product attributes is genuinely needed. The team rule is simple
  enough to enforce without governance overhead:
    IF money or user identity → PostgreSQL (Prisma)
    IF product catalog attribute → MongoDB (Mongoose)
